chapters.title: Chapter 5: Costs, Margins, and Taxes of Hedging in India

lessons.title: Lot Sizes, Margins, and Physical Settlement: Practical Rules for Hedgers

children.text: Most hedges fail for boring reasons. The portfolio was smaller than one lot. The margin on a short call ballooned in a rally and the broker squared off the position. A stock put was left to expire in the money and 400 shares vanished from the demat account on settlement day. None of this is about strikes or volatility. It is plumbing, and every hedger needs to know how the plumbing works before the water arrives. This lesson covers the three pieces that catch investors out: lot sizes, margins and settlement.

body.text: Buying protection needs only the premium. Selling anything, even inside a collar, needs margin that grows as the market moves against you. Knowing which side of that line your hedge sits on decides how much cash you must keep aside.

children.text: Lot Sizes: The Minimum Ticket

You cannot buy half a Nifty put. Contracts trade in lots, and the exchange sets the lot size so that one contract represents a minimum rupee value. SEBI raised that minimum sharply in its October 2024 measures for index derivatives, and exchanges revised lot sizes to match. For hedgers, the consequence is simple and important: the smallest hedge you can place is now much larger than it used to be.

body.text: Lot sizes are revised periodically as index levels change, and stock lot sizes change at each review. A hedge that was two lots last year may be the wrong size today. Check the current lot size on the NSE website before every new hedge and every roll, and recalculate your hedge ratio with it.

children.text: Margins: Who Pays What

markDefs.definition: Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk: the exchange's system for calculating the margin an option or futures seller must keep, based on how much the position could lose in a range of market scenarios.

children.text: An option buyer's risk is capped at the premium, so brokers collect that premium upfront and nothing more. An option seller's risk is open-ended, so the exchange demands
SPAN
margin plus an additional exposure margin, and recalculates the requirement every day. That is the whole difference between a protective put and a collar in cash terms.

body.label: The plain protective put has no margin at all
body.value: Pay the premium, and nothing further can ever be demanded
body.context: This is why a plain long put is the safest hedging structure operationally, even though it is not the cheapest. No margin call can force you out of it at the worst moment.

children.text: Margin can be met partly with securities rather than cash. You pledge shares, ETFs or eligible mutual fund units to your broker, the value is reduced by a haircut, and the rest counts as collateral. But SEBI requires a portion of your total margin to be in cash or cash equivalents, so pledging alone is never enough. Plan for real money in the account.

body.title: Which position can trigger a margin call?
body.question: An investor holds ₹32.5 lakh in index funds and hedges with a collar: two lots of long Nifty puts and two lots of short Nifty calls. The Nifty rallies hard. What can the broker demand?
options: Additional premium on the long puts
Additional margin on the short calls
Nothing, because the position is a hedge
Immediate redemption of the index funds
body.explanation: Long options never require more than the premium already paid. The short calls are the risk: as the index rises towards and past the strike, the exchange's margin requirement rises and the broker will ask for more funds. Index funds held outside the broker are not automatically available to meet it.

children.text: Physical settlement is where hedgers get caught. In the last few trading days before expiry, exchanges apply delivery margins on in-the-money stock option positions, rising in steps as expiry approaches, because a real transfer of shares and money is about to happen. An investor who bought a protective put purely for insurance, and who has no intention of selling the shares, can suddenly face a large margin requirement and then an unwanted sale.

body.title: The put that sold the shares
body.scenario: Suresh holds 400 Infosys shares and bought one lot of the 1,450 put as protection through results. The stock disappoints and trades at ₹1,380 in expiry week. Suresh is pleased that his hedge worked and plans to hold the shares for years. He does nothing. On expiry day the put is in the money, and his broker begins applying delivery margins two days earlier. After settlement, his 400 shares are gone and ₹5,80,000 has been credited to his account.
body.prompt: What went wrong, what were his options, and what should he do differently next time?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Nothing went wrong mechanically. His in-the-money long put was exercised, so he sold 400 shares at the ₹1,450 strike, receiving 1,450 × 400 = ₹5,80,000. The hedge paid exactly as designed.
2. But the outcome did not match his intention. He wanted insurance, not an exit. He has now sold a long-term holding, triggering capital gains tax, and must buy back at market price if he still wants the shares.
3. What he should have done: sell the put in the market before expiry week. He would have received its market value, roughly the ₹70 of intrinsic value plus whatever time value remained, and kept his shares.
4. He would also have avoided the delivery margins applied in the final days, which can be a shock if the account has little spare cash.
5. The rule: physically settled stock options should be closed before expiry week unless you genuinely want the delivery. Set a calendar reminder for the week before expiry, not expiry day itself.
The lesson: a stock option hedge has two exits. Choose deliberately, well before the exchange chooses for you.

body.title: The minimum hedgeable portfolio
body.prompt: The Nifty is at 24,500 and the lot size is 65. What is the notional value of one lot, in rupees? This is roughly the smallest beta-weighted exposure that can be hedged without a large over-hedge.
body.explanation: 65 × 24,500 = ₹15,92,500. An investor with ₹8 lakh of exposure buying one lot would be about 199% hedged, which is a bet on a fall rather than a hedge. Recalculate this figure every time the Nifty level or the lot size changes.

body.title: Collateral basics
body.textWithBlank: When you pledge shares to meet margin, the broker values them after applying a ___, and SEBI still requires part of the margin in cash or cash equivalents.
body.explanation: The haircut is a discount to market value that protects the broker if the pledged security falls. It varies by security, and volatile stocks get larger haircuts.

children.text: Five Practical Rules
Check the lot size before every hedge and every roll.
It changes, and your hedge ratio changes with it.
If you sell anything, keep a cash buffer.
Size it for the loss on the short leg if the market moves 10% against you, not just for today's margin.
Close stock options before expiry week.
Unless you actually want to buy or sell the shares at the strike.
Do not pledge your entire portfolio.
Cash equivalents are required alongside pledged securities, and pledged units are harder to redeem in a hurry.
Trade the liquid contracts.
Nifty monthly options have depth across strikes. Thin contracts cost you on entry, on exit and most of all in a panic.

You initiate a pledge request in your broker's app, selecting the shares, ETFs or eligible mutual fund units and the quantity. The depository, CDSL or NSDL, sends you a link or one-time password to authorise it, and the securities stay in your demat account but are marked as pledged. You keep dividends and any price gains.

The broker gives you collateral value after a haircut, which is smaller for liquid large caps and index ETFs and larger for volatile stocks. Two limits matter for hedgers: part of your margin must still be cash or cash equivalents such as liquid fund units, and unpledging takes time, so pledged holdings are not a substitute for a cash buffer during a fast market.

body.title: Operational checks before placing a hedge
steps: Look up the current lot size and calculate the notional value per lot at today's index or stock price.
Confirm your F&O segment is activated and your account has the premium, plus margin if any leg is short.
For short legs, run the position through your broker's margin calculator and check the requirement if the market moves 10% against you.
Note the expiry date in your calendar, along with a reminder one week earlier for anything physically settled.
Check the bid-ask spread and open interest of your chosen strike before placing the order, and use limit orders rather than market orders.

The exchange's scenario-based margin for option and futures sellers, recalculated daily.

points: Options trade in whole lots, and SEBI's larger minimum contract value means the smallest sensible hedge is now several lakh rupees of exposure.
Buying puts or calls needs only the premium. No margin call can ever follow.
Selling any leg, including inside a collar, needs SPAN and exposure margin that rises as the market moves against you.
Pledged shares can meet part of the margin after a haircut, but part must be in cash or cash equivalents.
Index options settle in cash. Stock options are physically settled, with delivery margins in the last days before expiry.
Close physically settled positions before expiry week unless you genuinely want the shares to change hands.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Lot sizes, margin rates, haircuts, collateral rules and settlement procedures are set by SEBI, the exchanges and your broker, and change over time. All figures here are illustrative. Verify current requirements with your broker before trading. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser for your own situation.
